pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/32678 - check this for a more detailed explanation

This PR contains breaking changes to the API contract exposed by `Microsoft.JSInterop`. We can do an announcement of these changes, but the main reason I think it's fine is that these are really internal layering APIs and will almost certainly not affect customers.

* Application developers definitely won't be broken or observe this as a change at all. It only touches things as far as JS runtime platform authors.
* People with custom implementations of `IJSRuntime` (e.g., mocks for tests) won't be affected because it doesn't affect the interface, only our implementations.
* The *only* people who should be affected are people who have genuinely made a custom `JSRuntime` subclass that actually talks to a real JS runtime. I'm not aware of anybody apart from us who has done that. I even checked the bUnit source code and it doesn't do this (it has a fake implementation of `IJSInProcessRuntime`, which won't be affected by this PR).

### Changes to the cross-layer API contract

 * `DotNetInvocationResult`'s `object Result` property is replaced by `string ResultJson`
   * Reason: This is the core objective of the PR, to correctly align "JS-to-.NET return value representation" with the other parts of the JSInterop contract. See #32678 for more.
 * `DotNetInvocationResult`'s constructors are now private
   * Reason: One of them has to change anyway because we now need to deal with a JSON string instead of an arbitrary result object. I can't see any good reason for them to be public. They are never used outside the `JSInterop` project in our code AFAIK, and I can't think of any reason someone external would want to use them. From searching the web, I can't see any evidence that anyone else is using them. They should always have been private AFAIK.
 * The JS-side `DotNet.parseJsonWithRevivers` export is no longer exported.
   * Reason: it was only exported before to work around our layering problem which this PR fixes. I can't think of any reason why someone would want it use it externally, because that implies they are somehow receiving JSON that was serialized by JSInterop, but that goes directly to framework code without an option to put your code in the middle. If we later discover some reason to export this we can do so, but right now AFAIK this has no reason to be public and nobody would be using it.

All three of these are tidying things up. Also the WebAssembly JSInterop mechanism now does less JSON serialization than before and avoids doing interop-within-interop for returning JS-to-.NET call results.

issue_context.title: Fix JSInterop layering mistake around JSON serialization of results
issue_context.body:
The intent for JSInterop is that it encapsulates the rules and semantics of JSON serialization for parameters and result values. Each hosting platform (Server, WebAssembly, WebView) only needs to know how to transmit JSON strings, and can't control how that JSON is generated, hence there's never any risk that different platforms have different behavior or bugs because they are using different converters, for example.

This has all been working well for us, but I've realised there's a mistake. JSInterop deals with:
 * serializing .NET-to-JS params, and deserializing the result values
 * deserializing JS-to-.NET params, but **not** serializing the result values

This "not" part is the mistake. It should cover this too. The fact that it doesn't now leads to two problems:

1. For the binary-and-streaming interop work, it would leak internal concerns about this into each of the hosting platforms
2. For the S.T.J. source generator support, it creates an issue because the current call-result payload combines the user-supplied result into a single JSON blob with system-controlled data about the call ID etc., which means there isn't a single "context" class that could deserialize it all in a nice way.

To fix this I propose we have a breaking change to the JSInterop abstraction contract where we: (1) have it pre-serialize the JS-to-.NET result values in the same way it does everything else, and (2) split up the call result JSON blob into two parts - one managed by the system, and one that purely represents the user result type. This will allow us to support passing a serialization context or even entirely custom serialization options without risking breaking the call info data managed by the system.

Although this is a breaking change, the only people it would affect are people who have built their own JSRuntime implementation, which is very few people. It's possible that bUnit would need to react, but I wouldn't expect any applications to be able to observe this change.

If we are doing this, it should be really soon (like, first day or two of next week) to avoid blocking @TanayParikh's work on binary/streaming interop. I'm happy to do it.

review_comments: We didn't do this before but do we need to validate `IsInitialized` here?

TBH I'm not sure what useful thing we could do if `IsInitialized` was false. The code as-is would end up throwing a nullref, but I'm not sure how much it would help to throw a different error. As far as I know there's no case where this can happen, or at least it doesn't seem to have been a problem in any case so far.

Since the existing setup wasn't troubling anyone, I propose to keep this aspect of it as-is.
That sounds sensible to me. It looks like the `IsInitialized` attribute was added recently as part of the error boundary work anyways which would explain why it wasn't used here.
How do you feel about leaving the API on this type as-is but interpreting `Result` as a string value?
TBH I'd rather take the opportunity to clean things up as much as possible if we're taking a breaking change anyway.
Instead of doing marshalled-interop-within-marshalled-interop to return the results, it now uses the lower-level unmarshalled API to return the results. This eliminates some JSON serialization.

Unfortunately the parameter isn't called `success`, so we can't do that. It's called `arg2` :)

This test was a bit weird before because it looked as if it was testing how the results get marshalled and represented as JSON, but it never actually JSON serialized anything and was cheating by looking at the unserialized results directly.

I've changed it now (in fact, was forced to by the clearer layering) so now it actually does observe things about the marshalling. As part of this I had to change it from a hetrogeneous array to some new DTO so that S.T.J. could deserialize it.
